# 1. Introduction

## 1.1 Background and use case

Zurich has a large amount of motorized traffic, and traffic volume changes throughout the day and across locations. Weather conditions may also be associated with changes in traffic volume.

## 1.2 Objectives

The objective of this project is to explore traffic volume in Zurich during 2025 and investigate how traffic volume varies with time, weather conditions and location.

## 1.3 Research questions

RQ1. Temporal patterns How does traffic volume vary across different times of the day and days of the week in Zurich in 2025?

RQ2. Weather How are weather conditions associated with traffic volume in Zurich in 2025?

RQ3. Location How does traffic volume differ across traffic counting locations and directions in Zurich in 2025?

RQ4.Model To what extent can traffic volume be explained by temporal, weather and location-related variables?

# 2. Data sources

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(dplyr)
library(lubridate)
```

## 2.1 Inspecting the traffic data

```{r}
traffic <- read.csv("data/sid_dav_verkehrszaehlung_miv_od2031_2025.csv")
```

```{r}
head(traffic, n = 10)
```

The original traffic dataset contains German variable names. Before the analysis, the variables were renamed into English to improve readability and consistency throughout the project.

The number and percentage of missing values are calculated for each traffic variable. This helps identify variables that may require cleaning or special treatment before the exploratory analysis.

```{r summary of missing values traffic, echo=FALSE}
traffic |>
  summarise(
    across(
      everything(),
      \(x) sum(is.na(x))
    )
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "missing_values"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    missing_percentage =
      100 * missing_values / nrow(traffic)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(missing_values))

```

Missing values were identified only in Number_of_Vehicles. A total of 107,602 traffic counts are missing, corresponding to approximately 5.84% of all traffic observations. The remaining variables do not contain values encoded as NA. However, some character variables may use labels such as “Unbekannt” instead of NA, which will be checked separately.

```{r echo=FALSE}
traffic |>
  count(
    Vehicle_Count_Status,
    vehicle_count_missing = is.na(Number_of_Vehicles)
  )
```

All missing values in Number_of_Vehicles have the status Fehlend, meaning “missing.” Measured (Gemessen) and imputed (Imputiert) observations contain vehicle-count values. The missing-value indicator is therefore consistent with the traffic count status.

Some character variables may represent unavailable information with the label Unbekannt rather than an actual missing value. These values are counted separately.

```{r summary 2, echo=FALSE}
traffic |>
  summarise(
    across(
      where(is.character),
      \(x) sum(x == "Unbekannt", na.rm = TRUE)
    )
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "unknown_values"
  ) |>
  filter(unknown_values > 0) |>
  arrange(desc(unknown_values))
```

```{r delivery date, echo=FALSE}
traffic |>
  count(
    Delivery_Date,
    sort = TRUE
  )
```

Several character variables contain the label Unbekannt, meaning “unknown.” MSName and D4_ID are unknown for every observation and therefore provide no useful variation for the analysis. D2_ID, D3_ID, House_Number, and Elevation contain a mixture of known and unknown information. These values are not technically stored as NA, but they should still be treated as unavailable information when the relevant variables are analysed.

Delivery_Date contains the same value, 6 May 2026, for every observation. It appears to represent an administrative delivery date rather than the traffic measurement date. Because the variable has no variation, it does not provide useful information for the exploratory analysis or statistical modelling. It will be retained in the original data but can be excluded from the analytical variables.

These mentioned columns will be removed from the data set for the above mentioned reasons.

## 2.2 Renaming and cleaning traffic variables

```{r pressure, echo=FALSE}
traffic <- traffic |> 
  rename(
    MSID = MSID,
    MSName = MSName,
    ZS_ID = ZSID,
    ZS_Name = ZSName,
    Axis = Achse,
    House_Number = HNr,
    Elevation = Hoehe,
    Easting = EKoord,
    Northing = NKoord,
    Direction = Richtung,
    K_Number = Knummer,
    K_Name = Kname,
    Number_of_Detectors = AnzDetektoren,
    D1_ID = D1ID,
    D2_ID = D2ID,
    D3_ID = D3ID,
    D4_ID = D4ID,
    Measurement_DateTime = MessungDatZeit,
    Delivery_Date = LieferDat,
    Number_of_Vehicles = AnzFahrzeuge,
    Vehicle_Count_Status = AnzFahrzeugeStatus
  )
```

```{r remove the unusable columns, echo=FALSE}
traffic <- traffic |>
  select(
    -MSName,
    -D4_ID,
    -D2_ID,
    -D3_ID,
    -House_Number,
    -Elevation,
    -Delivery_Date
  )
```

## Traffic data dictionary

MSID：Unique ID of the measurement station. ZS_ID：Unique ID of the traffic counting point. ZS_Name:Name of the traffic counting point. Axis: The road axis associated with the traffic counting point. Easting: Easting coordinate. Northing: Northing coordinate. Direction: Direction of traffic being measured. K_Number: Road Number. K_Name: Road Name. Number_of_Detectors:Number of Detectors. D1_ID:ID of the first detector. Measurement_DateTime: Date and exact time of measurement. Number_of_Vehicles: Number of vehicles detected during the measurement period. Vehicle_Count_Status: Quality or availability of the vehicle count data. (e.g., Gemessen → Measured;Fehlend → Missing;Imputiert → Imputed)

## 2.3 Preparing traffic date and time

The traffic timestamp is stored as a character variable. To prepare the data for the hourly merge and temporal analysis, three new variables are created: join_hour for merging the datasets, date for the calendar date, and hour for the hour of the day.

```{r echo=FALSE}
traffic <- traffic |>
  mutate(
    join_hour = substr(Measurement_DateTime, 1, 13),
    date = as.Date(substr(Measurement_DateTime, 1, 10)),
    hour = as.integer(substr(Measurement_DateTime, 12, 13))
  )
```

The original traffic timestamp and the newly created time variables are displayed together to verify that they were extracted correctly.

```{r echo=FALSE}
traffic |>
  select(
    Measurement_DateTime,
    join_hour,
    date,
    hour
  ) |>
  head(10)
```

The classes of the new time variables are checked to confirm that join_hour is stored as character text, date as a Date variable, and hour as an integer.

```{r}
class(traffic$join_hour)
class(traffic$date)
class(traffic$hour)
```

The original traffic timestamp was retained. A common hourly key was created for merging the datasets, together with separate date and numeric hour variables for the exploratory analysis.

## 2.4 Inspecting and cleaning the meteorological and weather data

```{r}
weather <- read.csv("data/ugz_ogd_meteo_h1_2025.csv")
```

```{r}
head(weather, 10)
```

## 2.5 Renaming and cleaning weather variables

```{r}
weather <- weather |>
  rename(
    Measurement_DateTime = Datum,
    Location = Standort,
    Parameter = Parameter,
    Interval = Intervall,
    Unit = Einheit,
    Value = Wert,
    Status = Status
  )
```

```{r missing values check for weather, echo=FALSE}
weather |>
  summarise(
    across(
      everything(),
      \(x) sum(is.na(x))
    )
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "missing_values"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    missing_percentage =
      100 * missing_values / nrow(traffic)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(missing_values))
```

The weather dataset contains only 244 missing values, all in Value. This represents approximately 0.013% of the weather observations. Missing weather measurements are examined by weather parameter, station, and status before deciding how they should be handled.

```{r filter for weather, echo=FALSE}
weather |>
  filter(is.na(Value)) |>
  count(
    Parameter,
    Location,
    Status,
    sort = TRUE
  )
```

Most of the missing values occur at the Rosengartenstrasse station, where temperature and relative humidity are each missing for 102 observations. The remaining missing values occur only occasionally across other stations and parameters. Because the overall missing percentage is very small, the observations will be retained as missing values at this stage. No values are removed or replaced before the exploratory analysis.

## Weather data dictionary

Measurement_DateTime:Date and exact time when the weather measurement was taken. Location:Name of the weather station where the measurement was taken. Parameter:Type of weather variable being measured, e.g. temperature, relative humidity, or air pressure. Interval:Time interval over which the weather measurement was recorded, e.g. one hour (h1). Unit:Unit in which the weather parameter is measured, e.g. °C, %, hPa, or m/s. Value Measured Value:Numerical value of the corresponding weather parameter. Status:Status indicating the quality or processing state of the weather measurement.

## 2.6 Preparing meteorological and weather date and time

The weather timestamp is stored as a character variable and includes a UTC offset. To prepare the weather data for the hourly merge and temporal analysis, three new variables are created: join_hour for merging the datasets, date for the calendar date, and hour for the hour of the day.

```{r}
weather <- weather |> 
  mutate(
    join_hour = substr(Measurement_DateTime, 1, 13),
    date = as.Date(substr(Measurement_DateTime, 1, 10)),
    hour = as.integer(substr(Measurement_DateTime, 12, 13))
  )
```

The original weather timestamp and the newly created time variables are displayed together to verify that they were extracted correctly.

```{r}
weather |>
  select(
    Measurement_DateTime,
    join_hour,
    date,
    hour
  ) |>
  head(10)
```

The new weather time variables are checked for missing values to ensure that they were created successfully.

```{r}
weather |>
  summarise(
    missing_join_hour = sum(is.na(join_hour)),
    missing_date = sum(is.na(date)),
    missing_hour = sum(is.na(hour))
  )
```

## 2.7 Reshaping the meteorological data （long → wide）

The weather dataset is initially stored in long format. Each hour contains measurements for several weather parameters at four weather stations. To obtain one row per hour, each combination of weather parameter and weather station will be transformed into a separate column.

```{r}
weather_wide <- weather |>
  select(
    join_hour,
    Location,
    Parameter,
    Value
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(
    id_cols = join_hour,
    names_from = c(Parameter, Location),
    values_from = Value,
    names_glue = "{Parameter}_{Location}"
  )
```

```{r}
weather_wide |>
  select(1:8) |>
  head(10)
```

```{r}
weather_wide |>
  select(join_hour) |>
  head(10)
```

```{r}
weather_wide |>
  count(join_hour) |>
  filter(n > 1)
```

## 2.8 Checking the join keys

Check the time period.

```{r check range traffic, echo=FALSE}
range(traffic$join_hour, na.rm = TRUE)

```

```{r check range weather, echo=FALSE}
range(weather_wide$join_hour, na.rm = TRUE)
```

Both datasets cover the period from 1 January 2025 at 00:00 to 31 December 2025 at 23:00. The join_hour variable has the same format and overall range in both datasets, making it suitable as the common hourly join key.

Before merging, traffic hours are compared with weather hours to identify traffic observations that do not have a corresponding weather record.

```{r compare correspondace as traffic is the ref data, echo=FALSE}
traffic |>
  distinct(join_hour) |>
  anti_join(
    weather_wide |>
      distinct(join_hour),
    by = "join_hour"
  )
```

## 2.9 Joining traffic and weather data

Initially, the weather data contained multiple rows per hour because measurements were recorded at four weather stations. A direct join would therefore have duplicated traffic observations. After reshaping the weather data, each combination of weather parameter and station is stored in a separate column, resulting in one row per hour. The datasets can now be safely joined using join_hour.

```{r}
traffic_weather <- traffic |>
  left_join(
    weather_wide,
    by = "join_hour"
  )
```

A left join should preserve all observations from the traffic dataset. Therefore, the number of rows before and after the join is compared.

```{r}
tibble(
  dataset = c("Traffic before join", "Traffic and weather after join"),
  number_of_rows = c(
    nrow(traffic),
    nrow(traffic_weather)
  )
)
```

## 2.10 Checking the joined data set

The variables added by the weather join are displayed to confirm that the weather measurements were successfully included in the combined dataset.

```{r}
setdiff(
  names(traffic_weather),
  names(traffic)
)
```

The join added 25 weather variables to the traffic dataset. Each variable represents a specific weather parameter measured at a particular weather station, such as temperature at Heubeeribüel or rainfall duration at Schimmelstrasse. This confirms that the weather data were succesfully added.

# 3. Plots

## 3.1 RQ1 — Traffic volume over time

How does traffic volume vary across different times of the day?

################################################################
<Task Splitting>

- Around peak hours (e.g., 15pm–18pm), check whether location/direction differs. — Elif
- Trend to leave/go to Zurich. Friday evening: leaving Zurich; weekend morning : go to Zurich. — Elif
- Compare weekday (Monday–Friday) vs. weekend (Saturday–Sunday) changes/patterns. — Aki
- Compare seasonal (e.g., summer, winter, etc.) hourly changes. — Aki
################################################################


### Average Traffic Volume by Hour

```{r}
traffic_hourly <- traffic_weather |>
  group_by(hour) |>
  summarise(
    mean_traffic = mean(
      Number_of_Vehicles,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{r}
ggplot(
  traffic_hourly,
  aes(
    x = hour,
    y = mean_traffic
  )
) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Average Traffic Volume by Hour",
    x = "Hour of Day",
    y = "Average Number of Vehicles"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

This chart shows the average traffic volume by hour across a single day: ・Overnight low: Traffic volume is lowest between midnight and 4 AM, bottoming out around 3 AM (roughly 50 vehicles). ・Morning peak: Volume rises sharply starting around 5 AM, climbing from about 140 to nearly 390 vehicles by 7 AM, then levels off at a relatively high plateau (around 400–460 vehicles) from 8 AM to 14 PM. ・Evening peak: Traffic reaches its daily maximum around 16–17 PM (approximately 530–540 vehicles). ・Evening decline: After 17 PM, volume drops steadily, falling to around 180 vehicles by 23 PM.

Overall, the data shows a classic bimodal commuting pattern, with a gradual morning rise and a sharper, more concentrated evening peak — consistent with typical weekday vehicle traffic behavior.

### Weekday vs weekend

```{r}
traffic_daytype <- traffic_weather |>
  group_by(hour, day_type) |>
  summarise(
    mean_traffic = mean(
      Number_of_Vehicles,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{r}
ggplot(
  traffic_daytype,
  aes(
    x = hour,
    y = mean_traffic,
    colour = day_type
  )
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Traffic Volume by Hour: Weekdays vs Weekends",
    x = "Hour of Day",
    y = "Average Number of Vehicles",
    colour = "Day Type"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

This chart shows the key differences in traffic patterns between weekdays (red line) and weekends (teal line). ・Weekday traffic starts rising much earlier and more sharply (commute-driven), while weekend traffic rises more gradually. ・Weekday peaks (both morning and evening) are notably higher than weekend peaks, reflecting structured commuting behavior. ・Weekend traffic is more evenly distributed across daytime hours, lacking the two distinct peaks seen on weekdays. ・Both day types converge to similarly low volumes late at night, though weekends dip lower overnight.


## 3.2 RQ2 — Weather and Traffic Volume

How are weather conditions associated with traffic volume in Zurich in 2025?

################################################################
<Task Splitting>

- Hour × weather condition	Weather effect across the day
- Temperature vs traffic	Continuous relationship	
 

################################################################

### Does the association between temperature and traffic volume differ across meteorological stations?

```{r}
temperature_long <- traffic_weather_selected |>
  select(
    join_hour,
    Number_of_Vehicles,
    starts_with("T_")
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("T_"),
    names_to = "weather_station",
    values_to = "temperature"
  )
```


```{r}
ggplot(
  temperature_long,
  aes(
    x = temperature,
    y = Number_of_Vehicles
  )
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    se = FALSE
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ weather_station) +
  labs(
    title = "Temperature and Traffic Volume Across Weather Stations",
    x = "Temperature (°C)",
    y = "Number of Vehicles"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

## 3.3 RQ3 — Location and Traffic Volume

How does traffic volume differ across traffic counting locations and directions in Zurich in 2025?

################################################################
<Task Splitting>



################################################################


```{r}
traffic_location <- traffic_weather_selected |>
  group_by(
    ZS_Name,
    Direction
  ) |>
  summarise(
    mean_traffic = mean(
      Number_of_Vehicles,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{r}
top_locations <- traffic_location |>
  slice_max(mean_traffic, n = 20)  # Select Top 20 locations

ggplot(
  top_locations,
  aes(
    x = reorder(ZS_Name, mean_traffic),
    y = mean_traffic,
    colour = Direction
  )
) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Top 20 Locations by Average Traffic Volume",
    x = "Traffic Counting Location",
    y = "Average Number of Vehicles",
    colour = "Direction"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

## 3.4 RQ4 — Combined Traffic + Weather Model

To what extent can traffic volume be explained by temporal, weather and location-related variables?

```{r}
traffic_weather_selected <- traffic_weather_selected |>
  mutate(
    hour = factor(hour),
    day_type = factor(day_type),
    ZS_Name = factor(ZS_Name),
    Direction = factor(Direction)
  )
```

Model 01 — Time + Weather

```{r}
model_01 <- lm(
  Number_of_Vehicles ~
    hour +
    day_type +
    mean_temperature,
  data = traffic_weather_selected
)
```

```{r}
summary(model_01)
```

Model 02 — Time + Weather + Location   (maybe need to consider interaction???)

```{r}
model_02 <- lm(
  Number_of_Vehicles ~
    hour +
    day_type +
    mean_temperature +
    ZS_Name,
  data = traffic_weather_selected
)
```
